title: Sequential randomness certification against non-signaling adversaries
formal: Is the randomness certifiable from a single pure entangled pair of qubits universally bounded against time-ordered no-signaling adversaries, even when Bob measures his qubit arbitrarily many times? Precisely, does a real constant \(B\ge0\) exist such that \[H_{\mathrm{NS}}(P,\mathbf y^0)=-\log_2 G_{\mathrm{NS}}(P,\mathbf y^0)\le B\] for every finite sequence length, every experiment in the single-pair model below, and every fixed generation input string \(\mathbf y^0\)?
why: The question tests how much repeated randomness certification depends on quantum theory beyond no-signaling. It separates the physical resource available to the honest experiment—a single pair of qubits—from assumptions about an adversary. A universal bound or unbounded family would clarify whether recycling one entangled system can retain its qualitative advantage under this stronger adversarial model.
status_note: Checked on 14 September 2026. The source explicitly conjectures boundedness against no-signaling adversaries. The 2024 quantum-security result and 2025 no-signaling accumulation preprint do not establish a resolution with this single-pair resource and measurement model. No matching proof or counterexample was found in the bounded search; the new proofs were not independently verified.

progress.text: The source proves unbounded certification against quantum adversaries and conjectures boundedness against post-quantum no-signaling adversaries for its sequential setting.
Padovan and coauthors obtain quantum correlation and robustness results with two sequential Bobs; they do not establish security against the full no-signaling set.
Ramanathan–Liu–Wu report linear no-signaling min-entropy accumulation in repeated Bell tests. The single-pair resource condition needed to apply it to this question is not supplied.

importance.reason: A substantial foundational question about the relation between finite entanglement resources, sequential measurements and device-independent randomness. The difference between quantum and post-quantum no-signaling adversaries tests the assumptions behind an unbounded resource claim, with consequences for the conceptual limits of randomness certification.

sentences: A single entangled pair of qubits is measured once by Alice and repeatedly by Bob.
The question asks whether the certified unpredictability of Bob’s entire outcome string has a universal finite bound against an adversary constrained only by no-signaling and causal order.
The honest experiment uses just one qubit per wing, but the adversary is not assumed to be quantum or dimension-limited.
Alice may have more possible measurement choices as the sequence grows, and the full observed correlations are assumed known.
Unbounded randomness against quantum adversaries and general repeated Bell-test accumulation do not by themselves settle this fixed-resource post-quantum question.

definitions: Fix an integer \(N\ge1\) and a nonempty finite set \(X\) of Alice’s measurement choices. Initially Alice and Bob share one normalized pure entangled state \(|\psi\rangle\in\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2\), and no other shared quantum resource. Alice receives \(x\in X\), performs one binary measurement and outputs \(a\in\{-1,+1\}\). Its effects are positive semidefinite matrices \(A_a^x\) on \(\mathbb C^2\) with \(A_{-1}^x+A_{+1}^x=I\). Bob performs \(N\) binary instruments successively on his same qubit. At step \(i\), he receives \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\) and produces \(b_i\in\{-1,+1\}\). His instrument may depend on all his earlier inputs and outputs. It consists of maps \(\mathcal M^{h,y_i}_{i,b_i}\) from two-by-two matrices to two-by-two matrices, where \(h=(y_1,b_1,\ldots,y_{i-1},b_{i-1})\). Each map is completely positive and trace-nonincreasing, and their sum over \(b_i\) is trace-preserving. Completely positive means that tensoring with the identity map on matrices of any finite size preserves positive semidefiniteness. The output quantum register passed to the next step is only the same two-dimensional system. Local auxiliary systems may implement an instrument but are discarded within that step; no extra persistent quantum register or fresh shared entanglement is supplied. The recorded classical history is available to later Bob steps. There is no communication between Alice and Bob during the experiment. Inputs are chosen independently of the preparation and of any adversarial side information. Let \(\mathbf b=(b_1,\ldots,b_N)\), \(\mathbf y=(y_1,\ldots,y_N)\), and let \(\mathcal M_{\mathbf b}^{\mathbf y}\) denote the composition of the corresponding history-dependent Bob maps. The exactly known observed distribution is \[P(a,\mathbf b\mid x,\mathbf y)=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[(A_a^x\otimes I)(\operatorname{id}\otimes\mathcal M_{\mathbf b}^{\mathbf y})(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\right].\] The size of \(X\), the state and the instruments may vary with \(N\); in particular Alice’s input set is not fixed to two settings. Define \(\mathsf{NS}_N(X)\) to be all nonnegative conditional arrays \(Q(a,\mathbf b\mid x,\mathbf y)\), normalized for each input, with the following marginal constraints. The sum over \(\mathbf b\) is independent of \(\mathbf y\); the sum over \(a\) is independent of \(x\); and, for every \(0\le j<N\), \(\sum_{b_{j+1},\ldots,b_N}Q(a,\mathbf b\mid x,\mathbf y)\) is independent of \(y_{j+1},\ldots,y_N\). The last condition includes the joint Alice outcome and Bob prefix and forbids signaling from later Bob inputs to earlier outputs. Forward dependence on earlier Bob inputs and outputs is permitted. Members of this set need not be quantum correlations or admit any qubit realization. For a fixed publicly known \(\mathbf y^0\in\{0,1\}^N\), set \[G_{\mathrm{NS}}(P,\mathbf y^0)=\sup_{P=\sum_e q_e Q_e}\ \sum_e q_e\max_{\mathbf b\in\{-1,+1\}^N}\sum_a Q_e(a,\mathbf b\mid x,\mathbf y^0),\] where the supremum runs over all finite convex decompositions with \(q_e\ge0\), \(\sum_e q_e=1\), and \(Q_e\in\mathsf{NS}_N(X)\). The mixture identity holds at every input and output, and the weights are independent of inputs. The expression is independent of \(x\) by no-signaling. Eve knows the label \(e\), may choose a decomposition for the fixed generation input, and guesses the entire Bob string. Alice’s outcome is not revealed or conditioned upon. The certified randomness here is this raw conditional min-entropy, without smoothing, postselection or an extractor; all \(N\) Bob outcomes belong to the string. The two-qubit restriction constrains which observed distributions the honest experiment can generate, not the adversary’s decomposition. Exact correlations are assumed; finite sampling and a noise tolerance uniform in \(N\) are not additional requirements.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of a universal finite bound \(B\), or prove that the certified min-entropy is unbounded in this model. A negative answer to the boundedness question must establish that for every real \(M\ge0\) there exist a finite \(N\), finite \(X\), one entangled qubit pair, allowed measurements and instruments, and \(\mathbf y^0\) with \(H_{\mathrm{NS}}(P,\mathbf y^0)>M\). Different experimental designs may be used for different \(M\). Equivalently, a positive answer requires a uniform constant \(c>0\) with \(G_{\mathrm{NS}}\ge c\). The optimal numerical value of a finite bound is not requested. Security only against quantum adversaries, a bound depending on the sequence length, or accumulation using an increasing supply of entangled systems does not resolve this fixed-single-pair question.

context_blocks.text: A quantum measurement can produce an unpredictable outcome while leaving a state that can be measured again. The question is how much unpredictability can be certified from the observed input-output statistics of this repeated experiment, when only one entangled pair was initially supplied.

An ordinary random-looking output is not enough: Eve may know which hidden component of the observed distribution occurred. The guessing probability maximizes her success over all allowed decompositions, and min-entropy measures the resulting unpredictability of the whole Bob string.

Curchod and coauthors show that one pure entangled qubit pair can certify any finite amount of randomness against quantum adversaries using a sufficiently long sequence. Their concluding question asks whether a finite upper limit returns when the adversary is constrained only by no-signaling.

Their sequential construction increases Alice’s number of possible measurement settings as the sequence grows. Fixing Alice to two settings would impose an extra restriction absent from that result. The present card permits every finite input set while keeping Alice’s output binary and her quantum system a single qubit.

The adversary model is made explicit here by replacing the source’s quantum decomposition with the full time-ordered no-signaling set. Each component preserves separation of Alice and Bob and the causal order within Bob’s sequence. Its dimension and physical realization are unrestricted: the honest qubit promise is not trusted as a constraint on Eve.

Padovan and coauthors’ 2024 work studies one Alice and two sequential Bobs, with a quantum correlation boundary and improved robustness of randomness certification. Its quantum-adversary guarantee does not answer the post-quantum boundedness question.

Ramanathan, Liu and Wu’s 2025 preprint reports linear min-entropy accumulation against time-ordered no-signaling adversaries when Alice and Bob run a Bell test repeatedly with a prescribed nonlocal value in each round. That theorem does not impose this card’s single-qubit-per-wing resource and single Alice output. General sequential Bell-test accumulation therefore cannot by itself be treated as a resolution of the single-pair question.

Unboundedness would mean that experiments can be designed to certify any chosen finite amount. It does not demand infinitely many outputs in one finite experiment, nor a fixed noise tolerance as the target amount grows.
